brief.text:
Good morning. The only prices in today's data are bunker fuel — the fuel ships burn — and they are up at all four main hubs. VLSFO (very low sulphur fuel oil, the standard 0.5% sulphur grade) was 1,019.50 USD/t in Singapore, up 17.50 (+1.7%); 993.50 in Fujairah, up 9.50 (+1.0%); 850.50 in Houston, up 13.00 (+1.6%); and 794.50 in Rotterdam, up 16.50 (+2.1%). That matters directly when you fix a ship: bunkers are the biggest voyage cost, so a broad lift raises the freight number an owner needs to earn the same daily return. No benchmark crude or freight index has refreshed today, so this is the only live price picture you have.

On everything else, nothing printed today. Brent crude was 117.19 USD/bbl and WTI 103.88 on Friday 30 October, with the Brent–WTI spread at 13.31 USD/bbl on the same date. The Baltic Dry Index — a dry bulk freight benchmark — stood at 2,714 points on Friday 30 October, up 2 points (+0.1%) at that observation, with Panamax at 1,889 and Supramax at 1,865 on Friday; the Capesize index (Capesize being the largest dry bulk ships, roughly 180,000 dwt, mainly iron ore and coal) was last seen at 3,726 on Monday 26 October. Tanker TCEs — time charter equivalent, a voyage's earnings expressed as dollars per day — are five sessions old: VLCC AG–China at 1,287,851 USD/day and Suezmax W.Africa–UKC at 406,769 USD/day on Sunday 25 October. The data here does not show why today's bunker prices rose.

Running stories: Hormuz remains live, with gCaptain reporting on 31 October that strikes on shipping are hurting both sides as renewed attacks are threatened. The Black Sea drone attacks had no news today and are unchanged. On products, Russia has extended its diesel export ban through January, which is new and sits alongside the unresolved US–Russia Atlantic diesel question. US West Coast labour developed: a security workers' standoff now threatens LA–Long Beach after a 4 November deadline extension. New today, Taiwan says China's coast guard is harassing shipping off its east coast.

Watch two things. First, the 4 November LA–Long Beach deadline, which decides whether a large slice of US import capacity stops. Second, whether crude and the Baltic indices refresh after the weekend — several are days old, so any "move" you see next will cover more than one session.

storylines.title: Direct attacks on ships in Hormuz
storylines.what: Tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz, including explosives attached to a hull, and strikes on commercial vessels continue amid threats of renewed US action against Iran.
storylines.why_it_matters: Attacks on hulls raise war-risk premiums and crew-safety objections for Hormuz transits, shrinking the pool of owners willing to lift Arabian Gulf cargoes and supporting crude tanker earnings.
storylines.latest: gCaptain reported on 31 October that the strikes are inflicting economic pain on both sides as renewed attacks are threatened; trade press also describes Gulf crude moving around the strait.
sources: Shipping Strikes In Hormuz Leave Both Sides With Economic Pain
Ramble On: Who Pays the Freight?

storylines.title: Drone attacks on shipping in the western Black Sea
storylines.what: A Greek container ship sank after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria, the latest in a series of strikes in the western Black Sea this month.
storylines.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings from the region and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling there.
sources: Dockworkers Strike Continues Friday Against Arms Shipments

storylines.title: Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab transits and Gulf congestion
storylines.what: Hormuz recorded six VLCC transits on Oct 25, the most since Oct 17, with one VLCC through Bab al-Mandab on each of Oct 24 and Oct 25. Vessel waiting remains elevated across the Arabian Gulf, with 265 dry bulk vessels waiting as of 28 October and Fujairah holding 28% of them.
storylines.why_it_matters: Transit counts and waiting times show whether ships route through or around high-risk waters, changing voyage lengths, tonne-mile demand and effective fleet supply.
storylines.latest: Trade press notes Gulf crude continuing to move around the strait as China's stockpile cushion draws down.
sources: Ramble On: Who Pays the Freight?

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia agreement on supplying extra diesel to the US market has met political opposition, while Russia's government has extended a general ban on most diesel exports until the end of January, with some volumes still allowed to flow.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment patterns.
storylines.latest: Russia extended its diesel export ban through January, reported 31 October.
sources: Russia Extends Ban On Most Diesel Exports Through January

storylines.title: Port labour disruption in the US and Europe
storylines.what: A contract standoff involving 250 security workers threatens to freeze operations across Los Angeles and Long Beach terminals after a 4 November deadline extension, while dockworkers struck across Europe and beyond on Friday over arms shipments through their ports.
storylines.why_it_matters: Labour action at container and ferry berths disrupts berthing schedules and cargo flows, and the unresolved US West Coast dispute leaves a large share of US import capacity exposed to stoppage.
storylines.latest: The LA-Long Beach dispute now centres on 250 security workers with a 4 November deadline extension.
sources: Impending strike threatens LA-LB ports container flow

storylines.what: Taiwan's Coast Guard says China's Coast Guard is harassing shipping with a patrol off Taiwan's east coast and asserting what Taipei calls a fictional jurisdiction, and has sent its own ships in response.
storylines.why_it_matters: Interference with commercial traffic near a major East Asian routing corridor can affect transit decisions, insurance and schedules for ships serving North Asia.

storylines.what: Taiwan's Coast Guard says China's Coast Guard is harassing shipping with a patrol off Taiwan's east coast and asserting what Taipei calls a fictional jurisdiction, and has sent its own ships in response.
storylines.why_it_matters: Interference with commercial traffic near a major East Asian routing corridor can affect transit decisions, insurance and schedules for ships serving North Asia.
storylines.latest: Taiwan publicly accused China's Coast Guard of harassing shipping on 1 November.
sources: Taiwan Says China Harassing Shipping With East Coast Patrol
